title: Accompany a singer
summary: Hold the chords steady underneath while a family member, or a recording, sings the tune on top.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil
a family member willing to sing, or a recording of a simple tune to sing along with

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard from middle C. C4, E4 and G4 are highlighted as an example chord, standing for the steady chord pattern held underneath while a singer, live or recorded, carries the tune on top.

steps.title: Accompany a singer
steps.body:
Accompanying is a different job from playing the tune yourself. Your job is to be the floor someone else stands on: steady, out of the way, never louder than the voice on top. Bend your tempo to theirs, not the other way around.

1. Learn the chord pattern that sits under the tune, in both hands if the piece calls for it.
2. Play the pattern alone, steady, while humming the tune yourself, to feel how the two fit together.
3. Play while a family member sings the tune, or while singing along with a recording of it.
4. Adjust your tempo to match the singer's breathing and phrasing, since a singer cannot pause the way a metronome can.

A good accompanist is heard as a feeling, not as a set of notes. That is the opposite of most of what you have practised so far.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: the chord pattern alone, steady, while humming the tune
Sitting 2: play while singing along yourself, matching your own voice
Sitting 3: play while a family member sings, or with a recording
Sitting 4: the same, adjusting tempo to the singer, then once as if recording
An old piece played once, alone, as a change of pace

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Record the accompaniment with the singer, or with the recording you sang along to, in one take, hands in the frame.

extras.title: Accompany yourself, twice
extras.body:
1. Record yourself humming a simple tune, a cappella, no piano.
2. Listen back and play the chord pattern along with the recording of your own humming.
3. Try the same recording at a slightly slower tempo than you hummed, and follow it anyway.
4. Notice how much harder it is to follow a fixed recording than a live singer.

What to notice: a live singer can bend for you, but a recording cannot bend back.
